notes: PNM placed in ruling slot 3 (MD had it in 2). No real coalition partner existed in 1970; slot 18 holds the OWTU, the strongest non-party labour force. DLP takes slot 1, Farquhar's Liberal Party slot 2. NJAC in slot 5. ACDC/DAC (A.N.R. Robinson) and ULF are post-1970 and omitted.

0.name: Special Branch
0.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence arm of the Trinidad and Tobago police, inherited from the colonial order in 1962. On 1 January 1970 it is watching the campus radicals of St Augustine, the oilfield militants of the south and the young men drawn to the National Joint Action Committee, filing reports for the Prime Minister and the Commissioner of Police.

Its officers think in the categories of the Cold War: subversion, Cuban influence, communist infiltration of the unions. They favour emergency powers, preventive detention and close liaison with British and American services. Their leverage lies in information and in the readiness of a nervous government to reach for public order legislation.

1.name: Democratic Labour Party
1.text:
The Democratic Labour Party is the main opposition, formed in 1957 from Bhadase Sagan Maraj's People's Democratic Party and smaller allies, and rooted above all in the Indo-Trinidadian sugar belt. Weakened by defeats in 1961 and 1966 and by the long absences of Rudranath Capildeo, it is led in Parliament by Vernon Jamadar and torn by faction fights.

The party defends Hindu and Muslim Indian interests, the cane farmers and rural traders against what it sees as a Creole PNM state. It is cautious, pro-Western and wary of both Black Power and socialist experiments. Its strength is a solid communal vote in Caroni and Victoria, its weakness a habit of splitting before every election.

2.name: Liberal Party
2.text:
The Liberal Party was launched in 1966 by Peter Farquhar, a dissident from the Democratic Labour Party, to offer middle-class voters an escape from the communal two-party contest. It won no seats in the 1966 election and survives in 1970 as a small group of professionals, Catholic businessmen and French Creole families in Port of Spain.

It preaches constitutional government, civil liberties, non-racial politics and sound finance, and is firmly pro-Western. Its supporters dislike Williams's personal rule but fear the radicals more. Its leverage lies in newspaper columns, links to the Chamber of Commerce and the hope of brokering a broad opposition front.

3.name: People's National Movement
3.text:
The People's National Movement has governed since 1956, when Dr Eric Williams, historian and lecturer of the 'University of Woodford Square', built it into the vehicle of the nationalist middle class and the Afro-Trinidadian majority. Williams led the country to independence in 1962 and is Prime Minister on 1 January 1970, with A. N. R. Robinson among his senior ministers, as unemployment and Black Power anger build.

The PNM stands for planned development, industrial incentives, mass education and a mixed economy under a strong party machine. It is Western in alignment but jealous of sovereignty, having fought the Americans over Chaguaramas. Its leverage is the state itself, the civil service and the loyalty of the urban Creole vote.

4.name: Vanguard
4.text:
Vanguard is the name militants give to the hard Marxist core that has formed around the Oilfields Workers' Trade Union newspaper of the same name in San Fernando. Its cadres are shop stewards, teachers and returning students who read Soviet and Cuban literature and see the oil belt as the natural base of a working-class party, which Trinidad still lacks in 1970.

They demand nationalisation of Texaco, Shell and the sugar estates, an end to foreign bases and close ties with Havana and Moscow. Their influence runs through union education classes and strike committees, and they hope to turn the coming wave of protest into an organised communist movement.

5.name: National Joint Action Committee
5.text:
The National Joint Action Committee was formed in 1969 at the St Augustine campus of the University of the West Indies after protests over the trial of Caribbean students in the Sir George Williams affair in Montreal. Led by the student leader Geddes Granger and Dave Darbeau, it is turning campus anger into street marches in Port of Spain as 1970 opens.

NJAC preaches Black Power: African consciousness, unity of Africans and Indians against white and foreign capital, and an end to the 'Afro-Saxon' PNM elite. It wants the banks, oil and sugar placed in national hands and rejects both superpowers. Its leverage lies with unemployed youth, students and the radical unions.

6.name: Massa Day Done
6.text:
Massa Day Done is the war cry of the PNM old guard, taken from Eric Williams's famous 1961 speech, and has become the label of party veterans who remember the 1960 'March in the Rain' against the American base at Chaguaramas. In 1970 they sit on constituency groups and the backbenches, resentful that the base is not yet fully returned.

They are socially conservative and suspicious of hippies and Black Power youth alike, but harder against Washington and London than the cabinet. They want the Americans out of Chaguaramas, curbs on foreign capital and a disciplined one-party nationalism. Their leverage lies in the party's grassroots and its founding myths.

7.name: Balisier House
7.text:
Balisier House, the PNM headquarters in Port of Spain named after the party's red balisier flower, has given its name to the hard core of the party machine. Its organisers, ministers and constituency bosses see the growing unrest of 1970 not as a call for reform but as subversion to be met with discipline and patronage.

They favour a dominant-party state on the Third World model, with tight control of broadcasting, unions and the public service, and they distrust Western embassies as much as the radicals. Their leverage lies in jobs, contracts, the special works programmes and the party's grip on the police and the civil service.

8.name: Hosay Yards of St James
8.text:
The Hosay Yards of St James are the family compounds where Trinidad's Shia-descended Indian families build the tadjahs for the annual Muharram commemoration of the martyrdom of Imam Husayn. Brought by indentured labourers from India in the nineteenth century, the rite survives in 1970 as a small but proud Shia tradition in a Port of Spain suburb.

The yard families want official respect for Hosay, protection from carnival-style commercialisation and recognition of Shia Muslims alongside the Sunni majority bodies. Their politics are cautious and local, but the yards command respect across St James and serve as the natural voice of Trinidad's Shia minority.

9.name: Cedros Imambara
9.text:
The Cedros Imambara is the devotional centre of the Hosay commemoration in the far south-western peninsula of Cedros, kept by a handful of old Shia families of Indian descent. Here, in 1970, a few elders and young men reject the drumming and festivities that have grown around Hosay elsewhere and insist on purely religious mourning.

They look abroad for guidance, to the clergy of Najaf and to the Shia awakening led by Imam Musa al-Sadr in Lebanon, and dream of a community ruled by religious law. Few in number, their weight lies in piety, lineage and the authority of the imambara over its congregation.

10.name: Anjuman Sunnat-ul-Jamaat Association
10.text:
The Anjuman Sunnat-ul-Jamaat Association, founded in the 1930s, is the largest Muslim organisation in Trinidad and Tobago, running mosques, primary schools and a growing network of secondary education among Indo-Trinidadian Sunnis. It is recognised by the state in matters of marriage and religious holidays and speaks for most of the island's Muslims in 1970.

ASJA stands for orthodox Sunni practice, religious schooling and good relations with whichever party governs. It looks increasingly to Mecca and the Muslim World League for scholarships and literature, and avoids radical politics. Its leverage lies in its schools, its imams and a disciplined community vote in central and south Trinidad.

11.name: Darul Islam Brothers
11.text:
The Darul Islam Brothers are a small circle of Afro-Trinidadian converts in east Port of Spain who discovered Islam through Black Power literature, Malcolm X and returning migrants from New York and Canada. In 1970 they meet in rented rooms and prayer halls, reject both the Indian-led Muslim bodies and the Christian churches, and dream of an Islamic community of their own.

They preach that only an Islamic order can free Africans from Babylon, regard the PNM and its foreign patrons as illegitimate and admire armed resistance from Palestine to Algeria. Their leverage is small, but they recruit among unemployed youth and prisoners.

12.name: Islamic Missionaries Guild of the Caribbean and South America
12.english: Islamic Missionaries Guild of the Caribbean and South America
12.text:
The Islamic Missionaries Guild of the Caribbean and South America is a revivalist association founded in the 1960s by young Trinidadian Muslims frustrated with the routine of the older mosque bodies. It runs lectures, publications and summer schools, and by 1970 is sending speakers across Trinidad and to Guyana and Suriname.

Its members draw on the writings of Hasan al-Banna, Mawdudi and Sayyid Qutb, calling for Islam as a complete way of life and a disciplined, educated community. It avoids party politics but criticises secularism and Western materialism. Its leverage lies among students, professionals and the youth of the Muslim community.

13.name: Whitehall
13.text:
Whitehall, the stately mansion on the Queen's Park Savannah that houses the Office of the Prime Minister, stands for the planners, permanent secretaries and economists who run Eric Williams's development programmes. They draft the five-year plans, manage the Industrial Development Corporation and negotiate with the oil companies in 1970.

They believe in rational planning above party politics, a strong executive and pragmatic dealings with East and West alike. They want localisation of the economy, state shares in oil and sugar, and order on the streets so the plans can work. Their leverage lies in expertise, files and the Prime Minister's trust.

14.name: Sanatan Dharma Maha Sabha
14.text:
The Sanatan Dharma Maha Sabha, formed in 1952 under the sugar-union boss Bhadase Sagan Maraj, is the leading Hindu organisation of Trinidad and Tobago. It runs dozens of Hindu schools and temples across the cane belt and, in 1970, remains Maraj's power base even as his health and political influence decline.

The Maha Sabha defends Hindu religion, Indian culture and the rights of the rural Indian community against a state it sees as Creole-dominated. It is socially conservative, hostile to Black Power and communism, and pragmatic toward any government that funds its schools. Its leverage lies in the pandits, the schools and the communal vote.

15.name: Trinidad Chamber of Commerce
15.text:
The Trinidad Chamber of Commerce, founded in the nineteenth century, is the voice of the import houses, banks and oil and sugar interests of Port of Spain. Its leading members are French Creole, Portuguese, Chinese, Syrian-Lebanese and expatriate businessmen, together with the local managers of Texaco, Shell and Tate & Lyle's Caroni estates.

The Chamber wants low taxes, open doors to foreign investment, firm action against strikes and protection of property from nationalisation. It is resolutely pro-Western and anti-socialist. Its leverage lies in credit, employment and quiet access to ministers, and in the fear that capital will flee if the radicals win.

16.name: Trinidad and Tobago Manufacturers' Association
16.text:
The Trinidad and Tobago Manufacturers' Association was founded in 1956 by local industrialists who grew up under the tax holidays of the Aid to Pioneer Industries legislation. By 1970 it represents garment, food, assembly and construction firms that depend on state incentives but resent bureaucracy and union power.

Its members preach free enterprise, lower taxes, deregulation and a stable climate for private investment, and they look to the United States and Puerto Rico as models. They oppose nationalisation and the radical unions alike. Their leverage lies in jobs, the industrial estates and their seats on government boards.

17.name: Trinidad and Tobago Field Naturalists' Club
17.english: Trinidad and Tobago Field Naturalists' Club
17.text:
The Trinidad and Tobago Field Naturalists' Club, founded in 1891, is the oldest conservation body in the country, uniting amateur scientists, teachers, birdwatchers and foresters. In 1970 its members survey the forests of the Northern Range, the Caroni Swamp and the turtle beaches, and lobby officials quietly for protection.

The club wants national parks, protection for the scarlet ibis and leatherback turtles, and controls on quarrying, hunting and oil pollution. It is apolitical in tone and drawn mostly from the educated middle class. Its leverage lies in expertise, scientific reputation and access to the Forestry Division.

18.name: Oilfields Workers' Trade Union
18.text:
The Oilfields Workers' Trade Union, founded in 1937 in the wake of the Butler riots, is the strongest union in the country and the heart of the labour left. Since 1962 it has been led by President General George Weekes, who has made it a fierce critic of the PNM and of the Industrial Stabilisation Act of 1965 that curbs strikes.

The OWTU demands nationalisation of the oil industry, workers' participation, repeal of the anti-strike law and solidarity with the sugar workers and the Black Power youth. It stands outside both blocs. Its leverage lies in its grip on Pointe-à-Pierre and the southern oilfields.

19.name: Workers and Farmers Party
19.text:
The Workers and Farmers Party was founded in 1965 by the Marxist writer C. L. R. James, back from exile and estranged from his former pupil Eric Williams, together with the Indian labour leader Stephen Maharaj. It failed badly in the 1966 election and in 1970 survives as a network of intellectuals, union militants and cane farmers.

It stands for independent socialism, workers' self-organisation and unity of African and Indian labour, rejecting both Stalinism and the PNM's state capitalism. Its leverage lies less in votes than in ideas: James's writings inspire the campus radicals and the oilfield and sugar militants.

20.name: British Empire Workers and Citizens Home Rule Party
20.english: British Empire Workers and Citizens Home Rule Party
20.text:
The British Empire Workers and Citizens Home Rule Party is the personal vehicle of Tubal Uriah 'Buzz' Butler, the Grenadian-born preacher and oilfield agitator whose 1937 strike made him a national hero. Long eclipsed by the PNM, the Butler Party survives in 1970 as an aging band of loyalists in the southern oil belt.

It mixes evangelical fervour, devotion to the leader, nationalism and grievance against politicians who used the workers and forgot them. It distrusts intellectuals of every camp and appeals to the common man against the elites. Its leverage lies in Butler's legend, which every party and union still tries to claim.

21.name: Iron Hand
21.text:
The Iron Hand is the nickname given in Port of Spain to a circle of retired colonial officers, planters, ex-policemen and businessmen who meet in private clubs around the Savannah and talk of saving the country from 'Black Power anarchy'. In 1970 they have no party, only money, firearms licences and old connections.

They want emergency rule, the banning of radical organisations, detention of agitators and a strong man above the politicians. They admire white-ruled Rhodesia and the generals of Latin America and scorn parliamentary democracy. Their leverage lies in wealth, private security and friends inside the police and the regiment.

22.name: Trinidad and Tobago Defence Force
22.text:
The Trinidad and Tobago Defence Force was created at independence in 1962 from the Trinidad battalion of the federal West India Regiment and consists mainly of the Trinidad and Tobago Regiment at Teteron Barracks and a small Coast Guard. In 1970 its British-trained senior officers face restless young lieutenants such as Raffique Shah and Rex Lassalle.

The force is officially apolitical and loyal to the Crown and the elected government, but the junior officers are open to Black Power ideas and resent being used against fellow citizens. Its leverage lies in the only organised arms in the country and in its barracks on the Chaguaramas peninsula.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
The House of Windsor reigns over Trinidad and Tobago through Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Trinidad and Tobago since independence in 1962. Her representative, Governor-General Sir Solomon Hochoy, the colony's last governor and the first local man in the post, exercises her powers on the advice of Eric Williams's cabinet.

The Crown stands for constitutional continuity, the Westminster system, Commonwealth membership and the Privy Council as final court of appeal. Loyalism is strongest among older Creoles, the French Creole elite and civil servants. Its leverage lies in the reserve powers of the Governor-General and the legitimacy of the constitution.
